label: Building Tools
title: Building Tools & MCP Servers
subtitle: How to give an agent a new capability — from a lightweight one-file tool you write in seconds, up to a full, packageable MCP server that goes through Innovium's Packaging & Testing pipeline and is published for everyone. Every level shares the same core: named methods with typed parameters and a handler for each.

subsections.title: Governance comes first
subsections.description:
> ⚠️ **Governance is a core concern of building tools — not just packaging.** Every tool you build or wrap becomes a governed capability: it can be assigned per agent, each method set to auto-allow, require-approval, or disabled, and it shows up in `list_tools`/inspect. So how you bring a capability in decides whether the user can govern it.
>
> This matters most for an external MCP server: wrapping its methods into a proper tool is what places them under Innovium's permission layer — connecting to a raw external server and assigning it whole hands an agent ungoverned methods and circumvents the governance layer. **Prefer a governed wrapper over a raw connection whenever the user needs per-method control.**

subsections.title: One core, three levels — pick the smallest that fits
subsections.description:
A "tool" is always the same idea: a set of named methods, each with typed parameters and a handler that does the work. What changes between levels is only how the code is packaged and run. Choose the smallest level that fits.

| Level | What it is | Build it with | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. In-process tool | Inline JS handlers the backend calls directly | `create_tool` (default) | Self-contained logic in a few JS functions (string/number ops, calling our own API) |
| 2. Subprocess MCP tool | The same handlers, run as a spawned stdio-MCP server | `create_tool` with `runtime: "subprocess"` | You want real MCP-server behaviour (crash isolation, a standalone process) but the logic is still self-contained JS |
| 3. External MCP server | A real project (any language) with its own manifest, deps, tests | Scaffold a project (see below), then add/publish it | The capability is an existing program — a CLI, a code base, a Docker image, a remote URL — or it needs its own runtime (Python, etc.) |

The decision in one line: **can the whole thing be a small, self-contained JavaScript function (optionally shelling out)? → `create_tool` (Level 1, or Level 2 if you want a real server). Is it an existing external program, another language/runtime, Docker, or a remote URL? → build a Level-3 MCP server.**
subsections.mediaCaption: A decision tree: self-contained JS logic branches to create_tool (Levels 1-2); an external program/runtime branches to a Level-3 MCP server project.

subsections.title: Level 1 — a lightweight in-process tool
subsections.mediaCaption: A create_tool call with two methods and a handlers export, producing a ready-to-assign in-process tool.

subsections.title: Level 2 — a spawnable MCP server, still one file
subsections.description:
Sometimes you want the tool to behave like a real MCP server — run in its own process for crash isolation, or so a flaky/heavy handler can't take the backend down. Pass `runtime: "subprocess"` to `create_tool`. You write the exact same `handlers`; Innovium wraps them with a stdio-MCP entry point and runs the tool as a spawned server that speaks the MCP protocol.

```json
{
  "name": "CSV Cruncher",
  "description": "Parse and aggregate CSV in a sandboxed process.",
  "methods": [ { "name": "sum_column", "description": "Sum one column", "parameters": [ { "name": "csv", "type": "string" }, { "name": "column", "type": "string" } ] } ],
  "code": "export const handlers = { sum_column: async ({ csv, column }) => ({ total: /* ... */ 0 }) };",
  "runtime": "subprocess"
}
```

Use Level 2 when the logic is still self-contained JavaScript but you want process isolation. If the capability lives outside our app — a binary, another language, Docker, a remote URL — that is Level 3, not this.
subsections.mediaCaption: A create_tool call with runtime: subprocess, producing a stdio-MCP server file with a runAsMcpIfDirect entry point.

subsections.title: Level 3 — a real external MCP server
subsections.description:
When the capability is an existing external program or needs its own runtime, you build a proper MCP server: a small project that speaks the Model Context Protocol, with an `innovium.json` manifest so Innovium can discover, install, and run it. You do NOT use `create_tool` for this. Instead, **this skill ships a ready-to-fill scaffold** (a FastMCP + uv project) under its `assets/templates/` — see the "Level-3 scaffold assets" table in the skill index. Copy those files into the project folder (keep the layout), then fill them in.

A Level-3 server has three parts, all in the scaffold:
1. **Server code** (`src/<pkg>/server.py`) — declares the tools. In Python with FastMCP: `@mcp.tool()` on a typed function; type hints + docstring become the tool's schema. Replace the example `echo` tool with your own.
2. **`innovium.json`** — the manifest (next section) that tells Innovium how to spawn/connect and what deps it needs.
3. **The gates** — the scaffold's `scripts/validate_innovium.py` (manifest is well-formed) and `scripts/test_innovium.py` (the server spawns and answers `initialize` + `tools/list`) are the exact scripts Innovium's "Packaging & Testing" stage runs. Run them before you ship: `uv run python scripts/validate_innovium.py && uv run python scripts/test_innovium.py`.

Two ways it reaches users: put the repo on GitHub with an `innovium.json` at the root and Innovium's scan lists it in the marketplace (and it can go through Packaging & Testing → published), OR add it directly in Settings → Tools: Import Tool for a local server, or Remote Servers → Add Server for a remote one.

**Already-running MCP server the user has at a URL: use `discover_mcp`, not `create_tool`.** If the server is up somewhere reachable over HTTP or SSE, call `tool-management`'s `discover_mcp` with its URL (and an API key or headers if it needs them) — Innovium connects to it, discovers its tools, and registers them. Do not reimplement a running server as an inline handler; that turns a thin wrapper into a second, worse copy of a service that already works. `create_tool` takes handler code only and has no URL field, so it is the wrong shape for this. (A server the user runs as a local process — a command, not a URL — is still a Level 3 scaffold or a custom server added with Settings → Tools → Import Tool, not `discover_mcp`.)
subsections.mediaCaption: A Level-3 project layout: server code, an innovium.json manifest at the root, and validate/test scripts.

subsections.title: The innovium.json manifest (Level 3 contract)
subsections.description:
One file at the repo root tells Innovium everything. Innovium auto-detects version (from the GitHub release tag), license, repository, author, and the tool list (via MCP `initialize` + `tools/list`) — you never declare those.

```json
{
  "id": "cas-scifinder-mcp",
  "name": "CAS SciFinder",
  "description": "Search chemical databases via CAS SciFinder APIs.",
  "category": "data",
  "command": "uv",
  "args": ["run", "cas-scifinder-mcp"],
  "transport": "stdio",
  "env": [ { "name": "CAS_API_KEY", "displayName": "CAS API Key", "type": "string", "required": true, "sensitive": true } ]
}
```

Fields: `id` (stable, lowercase-kebab, never changes), `name`, `description`, `category` (one of `development`, `version-control`, `communication`, `data`, `knowledge`, `productivity`, `project`, `ai`, `cloud`, `simulation`, `other`), `command`+`args` (the binary to spawn), `transport` (`stdio` default, or `streamable-http`/`sse`), `url` (required for HTTP transports; for a purely remote server omit `command`/`args` and give only `url`), `platforms` (a subset of the six `<os>-<arch>` values: `macos-arm64`, `macos-x64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-arm64`, `windows-x64`, `windows-arm64`; all six if omitted), `env` (a schema Innovium turns into a config form), and `dependencies.runtime`.

**Pointing your runtime at your own directory (`${INSTALL_DIR}`).** Innovium spawns your server with the *user's project* as the working directory, not the directory your package was installed into. A runtime that locates its project from the working directory therefore looks in the wrong place — `go run ./cmd/server` finds no `go.mod`, and Cargo, .NET and Java fail the same way. Write `${INSTALL_DIR}` anywhere in `args` and Innovium substitutes the absolute path of your install directory at spawn, so you can hand it to whichever flag your runtime uses: `"args": ["run", "-C", "${INSTALL_DIR}", "./cmd/server"]` for Go, `--manifest-path=${INSTALL_DIR}/Cargo.toml` for Cargo, `--project ${INSTALL_DIR}` for .NET. Spell it exactly — a bare `$INSTALL_DIR` without braces is not a token and is passed through untouched, and so is `${INSTALL_DIR}` itself if the tool has no install directory, so a typo fails at the launch line rather than silently starting in the wrong place. You do not need the token for a `uv` server (Innovium already anchors `uv run` at your package) or for a `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs` or `.py` file named in `args` (already rewritten to an absolute path under it).

Dependencies are auto-injected from `command` — `uv`/`uvx` → uv (+ Python), `npx`/`node` → Node.js, `bun`/`bunx` → Bun, `docker` → Docker, `python`/`pip` → Python. Anything else your server shells out to (gnuplot, ffmpeg, a vendor binary) you MUST declare in `dependencies.runtime` with per-OS install commands — Innovium will not guess.
subsections.mediaCaption: The innovium.json fields with a transport reference and the command-to-dependency auto-injection table.

subsections.title: Releasing a new version: the review gate
subsections.description:
Your users get a new version only after someone else reviewed it on GitHub. To ship one: open a pull request, have a teammate approve its final commit, merge it on GitHub with "Create a merge commit" or "Squash and merge", then tag the merge commit and publish the release.

When Innovium scans your organization, it imports a release only if all of this holds:
- The tag points at a commit GitHub itself made and signed when it merged a pull request into the default branch. A merge made on your own machine and pushed does not count, and neither does "Rebase and merge", because GitHub does not sign the commits it creates.
- Someone other than the pull request's author approved it, on the commit that was merged, and that person is the repository's owner, a member of its organization, or a collaborator invited to it, whatever their access. On a public repository anyone can leave an approving review; those do not count. A push after the approval voids it, so get a fresh one before merging.
- Nobody's latest review still requests changes.
- The approver is not named as an author or committer on any of its commits. Those names are written into the commits by whoever made them, so this only catches the honest case, and a commit made under an email that is not linked to a GitHub account names nobody.
- The pull request has at most 250 commits, and GitHub lists all of them.
- Every commit on the default branch's own line since the last approved release is itself the merge or squash commit of such a pull request. A change made in GitHub's web editor, or pushed straight to the branch, holds every release after it. More than 100 commits in a line, or more than 1000 in all, since that release are too many to check.

A release that fails any of these is held, and the admin who ran the scan sees why. So is a release GitHub cannot be read to check.

Some versions are judged differently:
- A new tool's first release, from a repository the catalog holds no tool from yet, is held: there is nothing reviewed to measure it from, and code pushed straight to the default branch before it would ship with it. An admin publishes that first release by hand, and later releases are measured from it.
- A tool with no approval on record when the scan begins, and none added while it runs, is measured from its current version's tag, when that tag is on the default branch and carries exactly the files the tool ships. If the tag was deleted, moved off the default branch or now carries other files, or GitHub cannot be read to check it, the tool's releases are held until an admin publishes a version by hand, and later releases are measured from that version.
- An admin publishes a release held for either reason from the scan results: in System Settings → MCP tools → Scanner, run a scan, choose **Import this release** next to the held release, and confirm. The release is published as reviewed by that admin, read at the commit its tag names, so read its code first. The next scan pins the tag to that commit while it is on the default branch and carries exactly the imported files, and measures later releases from it. Managers do not see the action, and releases held for any other reason do not offer it. Older releases are backfilled into a tool's history only when there is an approved version below them to measure them from. Every later release is measured from the last approved one.
- Once a tool has an approval on record, a new release must be numbered as a plain X.Y.Z version, with no leading zeros, above every version approved when the scan began. One numbered below is held; publish fixes as a new, higher version. One that cannot be ordered against the approved versions, such as `v01.0.0` or any release when no approved version is a plain X.Y.Z, is held too. An older release backfilled into its history is measured from the newest approved version below it, like any release, including approvals made earlier in the same scan, and is held when there is none. So a reviewed release published between two scans is taken by the scan that finds it, even when a newer one is taken too; a release that scan misses is held in later scans, because the newer version is then on record.
- A version the catalog already served before this check existed is kept without a review while its tag is on the default branch and still carries exactly the files the tool ships. The comparison sees only those files, not dotfiles or binaries in the repository. If the tag is off the default branch or now carries other files, the version is held until an admin publishes a version by hand.
- A version's tag is pinned to one commit: the one its pull request was approved at, or, for a version kept or published by an admin, the one a scan first finds carrying exactly the files the tool ships. Once pinned, moving the tag holds the release; publish the change as a new version instead.
- A docker image is built only from a release approved on GitHub, and only when the release it was measured from was also approved on GitHub. A docker version kept by a file match or published by an admin, and the first reviewed release measured from one, are listed as waiting for a reviewed release, because an image builds from everything at the commit, not only the files the tool ships.
- Two releases that name the same version, such as tags `v1.1.0` and `1.1.0`, are both held. Delete all but one.
- If a direct push holds your releases, an admin can publish the held version by hand. Releases then resume from that version's tag, read from the tag `v<version>` or `<version>` itself rather than from its GitHub release, as long as the tag is on the default branch and carries exactly the files the admin published. A tag at other files never replaces what the admin published. While no such tag exists, `v<version>` and `<version>` name different commits, the tag is off the default branch or carries other files, or GitHub cannot be read, later releases are held.
- A tool takes releases only from the repository it was imported from. A tool with no recorded repository takes none from scans. If the repository moved, an admin changes the tool's repository first.

subsections.title: Recipes by scenario
subsections.description:
Map the user's request to a level and a manifest. For every case that needs a real server, start from the scaffold assets this skill ships (`assets/templates/`).

**A published npm MCP server (npx).** It already exists — you just register it. Copy the scaffold's `innovium.json` and set `{ "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@scope/the-server"] }` (Node auto-injected). No server code to write — drop `pyproject.toml`/`src/`.

**A CLI already installed on the machine.** Two options. Lightweight: a Level-1 `create_tool` whose handler shells out to the CLI. Proper: copy the scaffold and have `server.py` shell out to the CLI, with the CLI declared in `dependencies.runtime` so Innovium can check/install it.

**An existing code base in a GitHub repo.** If it can speak MCP, add an `innovium.json` at its root and Innovium's scan lists it. If it is plain library code, drop the scaffold into that repo and wrap its entry points as `@mcp.tool()` functions in `server.py`.

**A code base on the user's machine (needs copying).** Same as the GitHub case but local: copy the scaffold, point its tools at the entry point, and add it with Settings → Tools → Import Tool (a `command` entry) (or push to a repo and let the scan pick it up).

**A tool packaged in a Docker container.** Copy the scaffold's `innovium.json` and set `{ "command": "docker", "args": ["run", "--rm", "-i", "org/image:tag"] }` (Docker auto-injected). The container must speak MCP over stdio; no `pyproject.toml`/`src/` needed.

**A remote server someone else hosts.** No `command` — scaffold's `innovium.json` becomes `{ "transport": "streamable-http", "url": "https://api.example.com/mcp" }`, or add it with Settings → Tools → Remote Servers → Add Server. Supply an API key via `env` if it needs one.

**A server the user ALREADY runs (local command or remote URL).** Nothing to build — register it. For a remote HTTP/SSE URL, `discover_mcp` connects and lists its tools. For a LOCAL server launched as a command (e.g. `node server.mjs`, `npx -y some-mcp`) OR a remote URL, `add_mcp_server` registers and starts it — so the user never has to open Settings. Both are approval-gated (the backend spawns/connects), and the registered server's methods must be assigned to an agent with `assign_tool` before use.
